newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli device gives new life for old nappies.
newsitem.headline: Israeli device gives new life for old nappies.

text.p: Parents faced with the dilemma of using environmentally friendly cloth diapers or convenient paper disposables can look forward to a less-conflicted future thanks to a device developed in Israel.

The Diapactor takes used disposable nappies, removes the undesirable bits and converts the rest into pellets of plastic and wood pulp, said Alan Brazil, president and chief operation officer of Dia Tec, the company developing the device.

"We're taking something of a bulk and taking it down by 90 percent...We see the real ecology of it in solving the problem of dealing with four million tonnes of used diapers each year," Brazil said. "Those four million tonnes require huge amount of transport and landfill."
The Diapactor does not use chemicals or detergents, which would substitute one environmental problem for another. It is based entirely on a mechanical process.

"It cuts the nappies, breaks them up and separates the plastic," Brazil told Reuters recently. "All the plastic is heated and melted into small plastic plugs. The rest, which consists of human waste, pulp and chemicals, is sent into another separator which sorts out the wood pulp."
The Diapactor can gobble up as many as 60 diapers an hour, or 250,000 a year at full capacity, Brazil said.
The Diapactor was conceived by Yaron Cina, a father of four small children.
"The inventor...saw he was throwing out so much waste," Brazil said. "This is what he has put the last four to five years of effort and imagination into."

Twice the size of a washing machine and costing $20,000, the Diapactor is not for home use. Brazil wants instead to sell it to hospitals and other institutions and to what he hopes will be a nascent diaper-recycling industry.
Americans, he said, already recycle a lot of their garbage -- so why not diapers?
"You put out your tin, you put out your papers, you put out your glass," said Brazil. "Now you're going to put out dirty diapers. We'll collect and replace them with clean diapers."
He said a beta model for on-site testing will be ready soon and the first commercial models, for hospitals, will be on the market in about 18 months.
"They're falling all over themselves trying to get one," Brazil said.

Eventually, you could have a Diapactor at home, too. "We have in our planning a home model that could do about two an hour," says Brazil. The pellets would be redeemable for coupons to encourage recycling.
